identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Krishna Janmasthan (Krishna Janmabhoomi) in Mathura is venerated as the birthplace of Krishna. The complex houses the Keshavdeva Temple, a Garbha Griha traditionally held to mark the site of Krishna's birth, and the Bhagavata Bhavan hall enshrining Radha-Krishna and other deities, all administered by the Shri Krishna Janmasthan Seva Sansthan trust. The complex is immediately adjacent to the Shahi Eidgah mosque, and the two sites are the subject of long-running, still-unresolved litigation over the underlying land; that dispute is described here as documented legal history, without taking a position on it.

narrative.summaryIntro:
Shri Krishna Janmabhoomi in Mathura is one of the most revered Vaishnava pilgrimage sites in India, venerated as the birthplace of Krishna. The present complex comprises the Keshavdeva Temple dedicated to Krishna, a Garbha Griha traditionally identified with the prison cell of Kansa where Krishna is held to have been born, the adjoining Yogmaya shrine, and the Bhagavata Bhavan hall enshrining Radha-Krishna alongside other deities. It is administered by the Shri Krishna Janmasthan Seva Sansthan, a trust registered in 1951.

The site's documented history runs from ancient settlement and repeated medieval destruction and reconstruction through to the trust-led rebuilding of the 1950s–80s. The complex stands immediately beside the Shahi Eidgah mosque, and the historical relationship between the two sites — along with present-day claims over the land — is the subject of active litigation that remains unresolved as of the most recent sources reviewed for this record (mid-2025). That history and litigation are summarised neutrally below.
narrative.documentedHistory:
Archaeological finds of pottery and terracotta at the site have been dated to around the 6th century BCE, and temple structures are recorded on the site from antiquity; a temple is described as having been rebuilt by the Gupta emperor Chandragupta II around 400 CE, with further donations recorded in the late 8th century under the Rashtrakutas. Mahmud of Ghazni is recorded as having attacked and destroyed the temple in 1017–1018 CE, and a Sanskrit inscription dated 1150 CE documents the construction of a Vishnu temple on the site by one Jajja.

In 1618, Raja Vir Singh Deo of Orchha (Bundela) built an octagonal red sandstone temple at the site, which the French traveller Jean-Baptiste Tavernier described visiting around 1650. In 1670 the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb had this Keshavdeva temple destroyed, and the Shahi Eidgah mosque was subsequently built using the ruins of the temple's assembly hall. In 1804 the British East India Company auctioned the land. In 1944, Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya acquired the site with funding from the industrialist Jugal Kishore Birla; the Shri Krishna Janmasthan Seva Sansthan trust was registered on 21 February 1951, and construction of the present complex ran from 1953 to 1982, funded by the Birla, Dalmia and Goenka business families. The Keshavdeva Temple itself was inaugurated on 6 September 1958.

The temple's own historical account, published on its website, traces the site's sacred association further back, to the Treta Yuga legend of Shatrughna (younger brother of Rama) founding a town called Madhura after slaying the demon Lavana, and cites the 19th-century archaeologist Alexander Cunningham's identification of an ancient settlement centred on the Katra Keshavadeva area.

The complex sits directly beside the Shahi Eidgah mosque, and the relationship between the two sites has been litigated for decades. A 1935 Allahabad High Court ruling addressed land ownership at the site. In 1968 a compromise agreement was reached between the Shree Krishna Janmasthan Seva Sangh and the Shahi Eidgah mosque committee, under which the temple land went to the trust and management of the mosque to the Eidgah committee; the authority of at least one signatory to bind the parties has since been contested. Following the 1992 demolition of the Babri Masjid in Ayodhya, a petition was filed in the Mathura district court challenging the 1968 agreement and invoking the Places of Worship (Special Provisions) Act, 1991, which bars altering the religious character of a place of worship from its status as of 15 August 1947 (with an exception carved out for the then-pending Ayodhya dispute). A wave of civil suits followed in the 2020s. The Allahabad High Court ordered a court-supervised survey of the mosque premises in December 2023; the Supreme Court stayed that survey order in January 2024 and has since extended the stay while hearing appeals. In August 2024 the Allahabad High Court ruled that the underlying civil suits are maintainable and can proceed to trial, rejecting a challenge from the mosque committee and the UP Sunni Central Waqf Board; a recall petition against a related order was rejected in October 2024. In July 2025 the High Court dismissed a plea by Hindu petitioners to have the mosque referred to as a 'disputed structure' in further proceedings. As of the most recent sources reviewed for this record, the litigation continues and no court has ruled on the underlying merits of the dispute over the land itself; this account does not take a position on that dispute.
narrative.architectureStyle: Modern reconstruction (1953–1982) on an ancient site; the 1618 temple destroyed in 1670 was built of red sandstone in an octagonal plan

visitingInfo.dressCode: A travel-guide source (not the temple's own site) describes modest Indian attire as expected: men in long trousers or dhotis with shirts or kurtas, women in sarees or salwar kameez; shorts and sleeveless tops are described as not permitted, and footwear must be removed before entering.
visitingInfo.nearestAirport: Kheria Airport, Agra, 46 km; Indira Gandhi International Airport, New Delhi, 136 km
visitingInfo.photographyPolicy: Per a third-party travel guide (not the temple's own published policy), mobile phones, cameras and large bags are restricted inside the temple premises, with cloakrooms/lockers available near the entry point; the source attributes this to the temple's proximity to the adjoining Shahi Idgah. This should be confirmed directly before visiting.
visitingInfo.officialContactNote: The trust (+91 565 2423714, skjs.sewasansthan@gmail.com) publishes its own seasonal darshan and aarti schedule, but the version reviewed for this record was dated to an 11 April 2024 – 10 April 2025 cycle and had not visibly been updated since; its summer/winter hours also differ by about 30 minutes from those published by UP Tourism (see openingHours notes). Confirm the current day's timings with the trust before travelling. Entry involves a security screening, and mobile phones, cameras and bags are restricted inside the complex per third-party sources.

shrines.locationDescription: The main temple of the complex; the present structure was built between 1953 and 1958.

shrines.deityOrSubject: Site traditionally venerated as Krishna's birthplace
shrines.locationDescription: The inner sanctum traditionally identified with the prison cell of Kansa where Krishna is held to have been born; darshan hours here run longer than for the rest of the complex.

shrines.deityOrSubject: Radha-Krishna, with subsidiary images of Balarama, Subhadra and Jagannatha; Rama, Lakshmana and Sita; Durga; Shiva; Chaitanya Mahaprabhu; Hanuman; and Garuda
shrines.locationDescription: A hall whose circumambulatory walls carry frescoes of episodes from Krishna's life and copper plates engraved with the text of the Bhagavad Gita; its main shrine holds Radha-Krishna images described as about 180 cm tall.
Stands adjacent to the entrance of the Garbha Griha; the temple's own account describes it as the site where Yogmaya manifested.

festivals.significance: The temple's principal festival, marking Krishna's birth. The trust's own account describes a midnight celebration with 'Shri Ganesha and Navagraha Pujan' followed by 'Lord Shri Krishna's Prakatya Darshan' and a 'divine Janmaabhishek.'
Celebrated on the second day after Janmashtami; the trust's page states that 'lots of toys, sweets, toffees and clothes are distributed to the devotees.'
The trust's page describes 'elaborate arrangements... for Prasaad Bhandaara (free Prasaad) and Chhappan Bhog (56 types of sweets and savouries)' on this day.
Held on the second day of Aashaadh Shukla; per the trust, 'a grand procession of Lord Shri Jagannath is taken out from the Janmasthan complex, which goes through the entire city.'
Observed through the month of Shravan, including Kali Ghata on Shravan Shukla Ekadashi, which the trust describes as featuring 'light, sound, flowers and beautiful costumes.'
A full moon night on which, per the trust, 'an elaborate Maharaas programme is organised at Shri Krishna Chabutra.'
The trust's page states that 'a vast number of oil lamps are lit and placed in the courtyard of Keshavadeva's temple.'
Observed the day after Diwali; the trust states 'a grand Chhappan Bhog (56 varieties of sweets and savouries) is organised.'
The trust's page states that on this day 'Lord Keshavadeva is dressed up most beautifully in the attire of a cowherd.'
A spring celebration on which, per the trust, 'Shri Krishna is dressed up in yellow and made to wear various ornaments.'
The trust's page states that 'an elaborate procession of the Shiv Baraat is taken out from the Janmasthan complex' on this day.
Held on the 11th day of the Phalgun month; the trust states that 'cultural programmes from various parts of Braja are organised at the Janmasthan's Leela Manch.'
